title: Why do two very different starts end in the same place?
description: The trick of double, add four, divide by two and take away the start is run on the board with five, then with eleven, then with a letter for any number. Both numbers end in the same place, and the letter shows the start cancels. Keeko doubts that a bigger start must give a bigger end.
teaching_notes: One idea: write the start as a letter, follow each step, and watch the start cancel. Watch for students who think a bigger start must give a bigger end.

source: Try the trick (double, add four, divide by two, subtract the
video_script.why: A child sees that a letter-number follows every start at once, so one calculation explains the trick for all numbers.
video_script.substitution: the book's own trick with the starts five and eleven, then the letter ex
video_script.anchor: the think of a number trick of the book: double, add four, divide by two, take away the start
video_script.wrong_answer: eleven must end on a bigger number
video_script.wrong_move: believes a bigger start must give a bigger end, and forgets the start is taken away at the end
video_script.payoff_line: The start cancels out, so the trick always ends on two.
maths_rules: Start x: 2x, then 2x + 4, then (2x + 4) / 2 = x + 2, then x + 2 - x = 2.
The start cancels, so the end is 2 for every start.
video_script.design: One idea: a letter-number stands for every start at once. The trick stays on the board for the whole video; the two numeric tries sit above the letter try so the child sees them match.

beats.on_screen: the small title card From your book appears; four step cards line up: double, add 4, divide by 2, subtract the start; two start cards, 5 and 11, appear under them; the question is written in the anchor band

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.steps: the four step cards line up
marks.ask: the start cards 5 and 11 appear and the question is written

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about a think of a number trick.
<bookmark mark='steps'/>Double the number, add four, divide by two, and take away the number you started with.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We try it with five and with eleven. Where will each of the two tries end?

beats.on_screen: the trick and the two start cards hold still

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the letter x is drawn as a box that can hold any number; 2x and x + 2 are written beside it

marks.name: the letter x appears as a box that can hold any number
marks.twoex: 2x and x + 2 are written beside the box

narration: <bookmark mark='name'/>A letter that stands for any number is called a letter-number.
<bookmark mark='twoex'/>Two ex means two times ex, and ex plus two means two more than ex.

beats.on_screen: Given: steps double, add 4, divide by 2, subtract the start; starts 5 and 11
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the steps are double, add four, divide by two, and take away the start.
<bookmark mark='starts'/>The starts to try are five and eleven.

beats.on_screen: To find: where each start ends, and why

marks.find: the words where each start ends, and why are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find where each start ends, and why it ends there.
<bookmark mark='dbl5'/>Step one, start with five and double it to get ten.
<bookmark mark='add5'/>Add four to get fourteen, then divide by two to get seven.
<bookmark mark='end5'/>Seven take away five leaves two.
<bookmark mark='dbl11'/>Step two, start with eleven and double it to get twenty two.
<bookmark mark='add11'/>Add four to get twenty six, then divide by two to get thirteen.
<bookmark mark='end11'/>Thirteen take away eleven also leaves two.
<bookmark mark='letter'/>Step three, start with ex, because ex can stand for any number.
<bookmark mark='dbl'/>Double ex to get two ex, and add four to get two ex plus four.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Divide by two to get ex plus two.

beats.on_screen: subtract the start: x + 2 - x; the two x terms are crossed out

marks.cancel: the two x terms are crossed out and 2 is left

narration: <bookmark mark='take'/>Step four, take away the start, which is ex.
<bookmark mark='cancel'/>Ex plus two take away ex leaves two, because the ex cancels.

beats.on_screen: Answer: the start cancels out, so the trick always ends on 2

marks.both: the 5 try and the 11 try light up together

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The start cancels out, so the trick always ends on two.
<bookmark mark='both'/>Five and eleven both ended on two, and so will every other start.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 11 is bigger than 5, so a bigger end; the bubble is struck out when both tries show 2

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble about a bigger end appears
marks.fix: the two end boxes, both 2, light up and the bubble is struck out
marks.size: the cancelled x is shown fading away

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks eleven must end on a bigger number, because eleven is bigger than five.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the start is taken away at the end, and both tries left two.
<bookmark mark='size'/>The size of the start cannot matter, because it cancels out.
